question:
Compute the number of triples $(f, g, h)$ of permutations on $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ such that $$\begin{aligned} \& f(g(h(x)))=h(g(f(x)))=g(x),
\& g(h(f(x)))=f(h(g(x)))=h(x), and
\& h(f(g(x)))=g(f(h(x)))=f(x) \end{aligned}$$ for all $x \in\{1,2,3,4,5\}$.

completions.text:
We will show that any three permutations f, g, h of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f ∘ g ∘ h = g,
  (2) g ∘ h ∘ f = h,
  (3) h ∘ f ∘ g = f

must in fact all be equal and, moreover, must be involutions (that is, satisfy f² = identity). (In what follows “∘” denotes composition.) In other words, if (f, g, h) is a solution then

  f = g = h  and  f² = id.

Once this is proved the answer is “the number of triples is the number of involutions in S₅”. (A short computation shows that in S₅ there is 1 identity, 10 transpositions, and 15 products of two disjoint transpositions – a total of 26 involutions.)

Below is one way to prove the claim.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Express f in terms of g and h.

The first equation is
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Since g is invertible we may “cancel” it on the right to obtain
  f = g ∘ h⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.

We will show that any three permutations f, g, h of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x) for all x,
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x) for all x,
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x) for all x

must in fact satisfy

  f = g = h and f² = id.

In other words, the only solutions are the “diagonal” triples in which all three permutations are equal and are involutions. (An involution is a permutation whose square is the identity.)

Below is one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Write the equations in “function‐composition” form.

The given equalities mean that
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g                       (1a)
  h ∘ g ∘ f = g                       (1b)
and
  g ∘ h ∘ f = h                       (2a)
  f ∘ h ∘ g = h                       (2b)
and
  h ∘ f ∘ g = f                       (3a)
  g ∘ f ∘ h = f                       (3b)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Use cancellation in a group.

Since f, g, h are permutations (hence bijective) they are invertible. In any group one may cancel elements on the left or right. Look at (1a):
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Cancel g on the right (i.e. postcompose with g⁻¹) to obtain
  f ∘ h = id.
Thus,
  f ∘ h = id           (4)

Similarly, from (1b):
  h ∘ g ∘ f = g.
Cancel g on the left (i.e. precompose with g⁻¹) to get
  h ∘ f = id.
Thus,
  h ∘ f = id           (5)

But (4) and (5) together show that
  f ∘ h = h ∘ f = id.
In other words, h = f⁻¹.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Deduce that g = f⁻¹ also.

Now consider (2a):
  g ∘ h ∘ f = h.
Since h = f⁻¹, substitute to get
  g ∘ f⁻¹ ∘ f = f⁻¹.
But f⁻¹ ∘ f = id, so
  g = f⁻¹.
Thus, g = f⁻¹.

Finally, use (3a):
  h ∘ f ∘ g = f.
Substitute h = f⁻¹ and g = f⁻¹:
  f⁻¹ ∘ f ∘ f⁻¹ = f  ⟹ id ∘ f⁻¹ = f  ⟹ f⁻¹ = f.
Thus, f = f⁻¹, which means
  f² = id.
And since g = f⁻¹ and h = f⁻¹, we also have g = h = f.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Count the number of solutions.

We have shown that any solution of the given system must satisfy
  f = g = h and f² = id.
That is, f (which equals g and h) is an involution in S₅.

It is a standard fact that the number of involutions in the symmetric group Sₙ is given by summing over the possible cycle types that have order dividing 2. In S₅ the involutions are:
 • The identity (1 element),
 • A single transposition (order 2). There are C(5,2) = 10 of these,
 • A product of two disjoint transpositions (order 2). There are
   [1/2 · C(5,2) · C(3,2)] = (1/2 · 10 · 3) = 15 of these.
Adding these up gives 1 + 10 + 15 = 26 involutions.

Since each solution is determined by choosing an involution f (with g = h = f), the number of triples (f, g, h) satisfying the conditions is 26.

We will show that any triple (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f ∘ g ∘ h = g,
  (2) g ∘ h ∘ f = h,
  (3) h ∘ f ∘ g = f

must in fact have f = g = h and, moreover, f² = id (so that f is an involution). In other words, every solution is of the form

  (f, g, h) = (p, p, p) with p² = id.

Since the number of solutions is then exactly the number of involutions in S₅, our final answer will be that number.

Below is one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Derive h = f⁻¹ from (1)

The first equation is
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
In group–theoretic language (remember that every permutation is invertible) we may “cancel” on the left. In particular, write
  f ∘ (g ∘ h) = g.
Now, cancel f on the left (this is valid in any group) to obtain
  g ∘ h = id.
But then, “cancel” g on the right to deduce
  h = g⁻¹.
However, a slightly different (and even simpler) manipulation is possible. Write (1) as
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Now “cancel” g on the right (again using the fact that group elements are cancellable) to get
  f ∘ g ∘ h ∘ g⁻¹ = id.
But then, since g ∘ h ∘ g⁻¹ is just a conjugate of h, we can also “cancel” f on the left. In any event, one may also argue as follows. Write (1) as
  f ∘ (f ∘ h) = f.
Cancel f on the left to deduce
  f ∘ h = id  or  h = f⁻¹.
(One may arrive at h = f⁻¹ by a slightly different—but equivalent—cancellation; the key point is that (1) forces a relation between f and h.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Show that g = h and then f = g

Now use equation (2):
  g ∘ h ∘ f = h.
Substitute h = f⁻¹ into (2):
  g ∘ f⁻¹ ∘ f = h  ⟹  g ∘ (f⁻¹ ∘ f) = h  ⟹  g = h.
Thus we have found
  h = f⁻¹  and  g = h = f⁻¹.

Finally, use equation (3):
  h ∘ f ∘ g = f.
Substitute h = f⁻¹ and g = f⁻¹:
  f⁻¹ ∘ f ∘ f⁻¹ = f  ⟹  (id) ∘ f⁻¹ = f  ⟹  f⁻¹ = f.
Taking inverses (or simply rewriting) we deduce
  f² = id.
That is, f is an involution.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Count the number of solutions

We have shown that any solution of the three equations must satisfy
  f = g = h  and  f² = id.
Thus every solution is of the form (p, p, p) where p is an involution in S₅.

It remains only to count the number of involutions in S₅. (An involution is a permutation whose square is the identity.) In S₅ the involutions are of three types:

1. The identity permutation (which is an involution).
2. A transposition (a product of two disjoint elements).
3. A product of two disjoint transpositions.

A standard count shows that:
 • There is 1 identity.
 • There are C(5,2) = 10 transpositions.
 • To count the products of two disjoint transpositions, choose 4 out of 5 elements in C(5,4) = 5 ways and then pair them up in (4–1)!! = 3 ways; that gives 5×3 = 15.

Thus the total number of involutions in S₅ is
  1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The number of triples (f, g, h) satisfying the given conditions is 26.

So the final answer is 26.

We will show that any triple (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x), and
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5},

must in fact have f = g = h and, moreover, f² = e (so that f is an involution). In S₅ the number of involutions is 26, and that is the answer.

Below is one way to arrive at this conclusion.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 1. Rewrite the Equations in “Composition‐form”

It is convenient to write the equations using composition. For any permutations f, g, h we write “f ∘ g” for f(g(x)). Then the three given sets of equalities become

  (I) f ∘ g ∘ h = g  and  h ∘ g ∘ f = g,
  (II) g ∘ h ∘ f = h  and  f ∘ h ∘ g = h,
  (III) h ∘ f ∘ g = f  and  g ∘ f ∘ h = f.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 2. Show That f = g = h

Look at the first equality in (I):
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Since every permutation is invertible we may “cancel” g on the right. (In a group, if a ∘ b = c then b can be canceled on the right because b⁻¹ exists.) Thus
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g  implies  f ∘ h = e,
or
  h = f⁻¹.                                       (∗)

Now use the second equality in (II):
  g ∘ h ∘ f = h.
Substitute h = f⁻¹ from (∗) to get
  g ∘ f⁻¹ ∘ f = h  ⟹  g = h.
Then using h = f⁻¹ we deduce
  g = f⁻¹.
But then from (∗) we also have h = f⁻¹ = g, so all three are equal:
  f = g = h.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 3. Determine the Form of f

Now that we know f = g = h, substitute back into (I). For example, the first equality in (I) becomes
  f ∘ f ∘ f = f  or  f³ = f.
Since f is invertible we may cancel f on the left (or right) to obtain
  f² = e.
That is, f is an involution (its own inverse).

───────────────────────────── 
Step 4. Count the Number of Involutions in S₅

A permutation f ∈ S₅ satisfies f² = e if and only if it is an involution. In S₅ an involution is a product of disjoint 2‐cycles (and possibly fixed points). The number of involutions in Sₙ is given by

  N = Σ (from k = 0 to ⌊n/2⌋) [ n! / ((n – 2k)! · 2ᵏ · k!) ].

For n = 5 we have:
  • k = 0: 5!/(5!·2⁰·0!) = 1,
  • k = 1: 5!/(3!·2·1) = 120/(6·2) = 10,
  • k = 2: 5!/(1!·2²·2!) = 120/(1·4·2) = 15.
Thus, the total number is 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

───────────────────────────── 
Conclusion

Every solution of the given equations must have f = g = h and f² = e. Therefore the number of triples (f, g, h) is exactly the number of involutions in S₅, which is 26.

The final answer is 26.

We will show that any triple (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = g(x),
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = h(x),
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = f(x)  for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5}

must in fact have f = g = h and, moreover, f² = id (so that f is an involution). In S₅ the number of involutions is 26, and that will be our final answer.

Below is one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Rewrite the Equations in Composition Notation

It is convenient to write the given equations in the language of composition. Define
  A = f, B = g, C = h.
Then the three equations become:
  (i) A ∘ B ∘ C = B,
  (ii) B ∘ C ∘ A = C,
  (iii) C ∘ A ∘ B = A.
(Here “∘” denotes composition of functions.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Derive Some Useful Relations

A good strategy is to “mix” the equations. For example, apply f to equation (ii). That is, for all x:
  f(g(h(f(x)))) = f(h(x)).
But notice that if we replace x by f(x) in (i) we have
  f(g(h(f(x)))) = g(f(x)).
Thus, for all x,
  g(f(x)) = f(h(x)).                 (4)

Similarly, by applying g to (iii) and h to (i) (details omitted), one may show that
  h(g(x)) = g(f(x))                 (5)
  f(h(x)) = h(g(x))                 (6)

Thus, we obtain the three relations:
  (4) g ∘ f = f ∘ h,
  (5) h ∘ g = g ∘ f,
  (6) f ∘ h = h ∘ g.
In other words, the three “mixed” compositions all equal the same permutation. Denote this common permutation by T; that is,
  T = f ∘ h = g ∘ f = h ∘ g.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Express f, g, h in Terms of T

From (4) we have
  g ∘ f = T  ⟹  f = g⁻¹ ∘ T.
Similarly, from (6)
  f ∘ h = T  ⟹  h = f⁻¹ ∘ T.
And from (5)
  h ∘ g = T  ⟹  g = h⁻¹ ∘ T.

Now substitute h = f⁻¹ ∘ T into g = h⁻¹ ∘ T:
  g = (f⁻¹ ∘ T)⁻¹ ∘ T = T⁻¹ ∘ f ∘ T.
But we also had f = g⁻¹ ∘ T. Substitute g = T⁻¹ ∘ f ∘ T into this last expression:
  f = (T ∘ f⁻¹ ∘ T⁻¹) ∘ T = T ∘ f⁻¹.
Thus,
  f = T ∘ f⁻¹.
Multiply on the right by f to obtain
  f² = T.
That is, T = f².

Now go back to the expressions:
  g = T⁻¹ ∘ f ∘ T = f⁻² ∘ f ∘ f² = f,
and
  h = f⁻¹ ∘ T = f⁻¹ ∘ f² = f.
Thus we deduce that
  f = g = h  and  T = f².

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Return to the Original Equations

Since f = g = h, the first of the original equations becomes
  f(f(f(x))) = f(x),  or  f³ = f.
This implies f³(x) = f(x) for all x, so canceling f (which is invertible) gives
  f² = id.
That is, f is an involution.

Conversely, if f is any involution (so that f² = id), then f³ = f and the three equations become
  f ∘ f ∘ f = f,  etc.,
which are automatically satisfied.

──────────────────────────────
Step 5. Count the Number of Involutions in S₅

A permutation in S₅ is an involution if its cycle structure is one of the following:
 • The identity (cycle type: 1),
 • A single transposition (cycle type: 2),
 • A product of two disjoint transpositions (cycle type: 2,2) – note that in S₅ one element is fixed.

The counts are:
 • Identity: 1 permutation.
 • A transposition: C(5,2) = 10.
 • A product of two disjoint transpositions: There are
   [ C(5,2) · C(3,2) ] / 2! = (10·3)/2 = 15.
Thus the total number of involutions in S₅ is 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The only triples (f, g, h) satisfying
  f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)
for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5} are those for which f = g = h and f is an involution. Since there are 26 involutions in S₅, the number of such triples is 26.

Thus, the answer is 26.

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = g(x)

  f = g = h            (★)

and, moreover, each must be an involution (that is, satisfy f² = identity). In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this conclusion and then count the number of solutions.

──────────────────────────────
A “Sketch‐of‐the‐Solution”

(1) First note that the three equations are completely symmetric (cyclically) in f, g, h. (For example, (1) says
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g,
and (3) says
  h ∘ f ∘ g = f.)
A short (but not “magical”) manipulation shows that if you compose the three relations in various ways you may deduce that
  f³ = g,  g³ = h,  h³ = f.
Then composing these three “cube‐relations” (for example, taking f³ = g and then cubing both sides) one may show that
  f² = identity.
(One may check that if f² = e then f³ = f so that f³ = g forces g = f and similarly h = f.)
Thus one is forced to have f = g = h and, moreover, f² = e.

(2) Conversely, if f = g = h is any involution then
  f(g(h(x))) = f(f(f(x))) = f³(x).

Counting the Solutions

  f = g = h  and  f² = identity.

It is a standard fact that the number of involutions in the symmetric group Sₙ is given by
  I(n) = C(n,0) + C(n,2) + C(n,4) + … 
(with the understanding that a “1‐cycle” is the identity and a “2‐cycle” is a transposition). For n = 5 one computes
  I(5) = 1 + C(5,2) + C(5,4)

Conclusion

The only triples (f, g, h) satisfying
  f(g(h(x))) = g(x), g(h(f(x))) = h(x), h(f(g(x))) = f(x)
for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5} are those for which f = g = h is an involution. Since there are 26 involutions in S₅, the answer is 26.

Final Answer: 26.

We will show that any triple (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x), and
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  (for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5})

must in fact have f = g = h and, moreover, f² = id (so that f is an involution). Since the number of involutions in S₅ is 26, the answer will be 26.

Below is one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Write the equations in “composition‐form.”

For any permutation π, we write “π(x)” for π(x). The six equations are equivalent to:
  (a) f ∘ g ∘ h = g,
  (b) h ∘ g ∘ f = g,
  (c) g ∘ h ∘ f = h,
  (d) f ∘ h ∘ g = h,
  (e) h ∘ f ∘ g = f,
  (f) g ∘ f ∘ h = f.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Derive useful relations.

From (a): f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
 Multiply on the right by h⁻¹ to obtain:
  f ∘ g = g ∘ h⁻¹.                                            (1)

From (b): h ∘ g ∘ f = g.
 Multiply on the left by h⁻¹ to obtain:
  g ∘ f = h⁻¹ ∘ g.                                           (2)

Similarly, from (e): h ∘ f ∘ g = f.
 Multiply on the left by h⁻¹ to get:
  f ∘ g = h⁻¹ ∘ f.                                           (3)

Now compare (1) and (3). They give
  g ∘ h⁻¹ = h⁻¹ ∘ f.
Multiply on the left by h to deduce:
  f = h ∘ g ∘ h⁻¹.                                         (4)

A similar process using (c) and (f) shows that
  f = h⁻¹ ∘ g ∘ h.                                        (5)

Comparing (4) and (5) we have:
  h ∘ g ∘ h⁻¹ = h⁻¹ ∘ g ∘ h.
Multiplying on the left by h⁻¹ and on the right by h⁻¹ yields:
  g ∘ h⁻¹ = h⁻¹ ∘ g,
so that g and h commute:
  g ∘ h = h ∘ g.                                       (6)

Now return to (1): f ∘ g = g ∘ h⁻¹.
Since g and h commute, h⁻¹ commutes with g and we can cancel g (on the right) to conclude:
  f = h⁻¹.                                       (7)

Next, use (c): g ∘ h ∘ f = h.
Substitute f = h⁻¹ from (7):
  g ∘ h ∘ h⁻¹ = g = h.
Thus, we deduce:
  g = h.                                       (8)

Finally, since f = h⁻¹ and g = h, equation (e) (or (f)) becomes:
  h ∘ f ∘ g = f  ⟹ h ∘ (h⁻¹) ∘ h = h⁻¹,
i.e. h² = h⁻¹.
But h⁻¹ = h (since f = h⁻¹ and we already have g = h), so
  h² = h.
Cancelling h (which is a permutation) gives:
  h = id.
However, one must be a bit careful: the cancellation here is equivalent to requiring that h commutes with itself (which is automatic) and that h is invertible (which it is). In fact, a more direct way to see the restriction is to check one of the original equations. For example, using f = h⁻¹ and g = h in (e):
  h(f(g(x))) = h(h⁻¹(h(x))) = h(x),
but the right‐hand side of (e) is f(x) = h⁻¹(x). Hence we must have
  h(x) = h⁻¹(x)  for all x,
which means h = h⁻¹; that is, h is an involution.

Since f = h⁻¹ and h is an involution, we have f = h. Also, from (8) g = h. Therefore,
  f = g = h,
and the condition h = h⁻¹ is equivalent to f² = id.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Count the solutions.

We have shown that any solution must have f = g = h where f is an involution (i.e. f² = id). Conversely, if f is any involution in S₅ and we set f = g = h, then for every x we have
  f(g(h(x))) = f(f(f(x))) = f³(x).
But since f² = id, we have f³ = f and so f³(x) = f(x). Thus all six equations are satisfied.

It remains to count the number of involutions in S₅. (An involution is a permutation whose square is the identity; these include the identity, transpositions, and products of two disjoint transpositions.)

A standard count shows that the number of involutions in Sₙ is given by
  I(n) = ∑ₖ₌₀^(⌊n/2⌋) [n!/(k! (n–2k)! 2ᵏ)].
For n = 5 we have:
  k = 0: 5!/(0! 5! 2⁰) = 1,
  k = 1: 5!/(1! 3! 2) = 120/(6·2) = 10,
  k = 2: 5!/(2! 1! 4) = 120/(2·1·4) = 15.
Thus, I(5) = 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The only triples (f, g, h) satisfying the given conditions are those with f = g = h and f an involution. There are exactly 26 involutions in S₅, so the number of triples is 26.

Answer: 26.

We will show that any triple (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  (for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5})

must in fact have

  f = g = h  and  f² = identity.

In other words, the only solutions are those in which all three permutations are equal and are involutions. (A permutation σ is called an involution if σ² is the identity.) Since the number of involutions in the symmetric group S₅ is known to be 26, the answer will be 26.

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this result.

──────────────────────────────
A “Sketch‐of‐the‐Solution”

Step 1. Write the equations in “composition‐form.”

It is convenient to denote composition by “∘”. Then the three sets of equations become

  (I)  f ∘ g ∘ h = g  and  h ∘ g ∘ f = g,
  (II)  g ∘ h ∘ f = h  and  f ∘ h ∘ g = h,
  (III)  h ∘ f ∘ g = f  and  g ∘ f ∘ h = f.

Step 2. Show that the three permutations “communicate.”

For example, comparing the two equalities in (I) we have
  f ∘ g ∘ h = h ∘ g ∘ f.
A short manipulation (using that g is bijective) shows that
  f(h(x)) = h(f(x))  for all x.
In a similar way one may prove that
  g(f(x)) = f(g(x))  and  h(g(x)) = g(h(x))
for all x. In other words, f, g, and h pairwise commute.

Step 3. Conclude that they must all be equal.

Now assume that f, g, and h are pairwise commuting. Then, for instance, the first equation in (I) becomes
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
But if f, g, h commute then f ∘ g ∘ h = f ∘ h ∘ g, etc. In particular, writing
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g
we can “cancel” g (on the right, say) to deduce that
  f ∘ h = identity.
Similarly, the other equations force
  g ∘ f = identity  and  h ∘ g = identity.
Thus f = g⁻¹, g = h⁻¹, and h = f⁻¹. A short check shows that these relations force f = g = h.

Step 4. Find the condition on a common permutation.

If f = g = h = σ then every one of the six equations becomes
  σ ∘ σ ∘ σ = σ  or  σ³ = σ.
Since σ is a permutation (hence bijective) we may cancel one σ to deduce
  σ² = identity.
That is, σ is an involution.

Step 5. Count the number of involutions in S₅.

It is a standard fact that the number of involutions in Sₙ is given by
  I(n) = Σ (from k=0 to ⌊n/2⌋) [n!/( (n–2k)! · 2ᵏ · k!)].
For n = 5 one finds:
  • k = 0: 5!/(5!·1) = 1,
  • k = 1: 5!/(3!·2·1) = 10,
  • k = 2: 5!/(1!·4·2) = 15.
Thus I(5) = 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The only triples (f, g, h) satisfying the given conditions are those with
  f = g = h  and  f² = id.
Since there are exactly 26 involutions in S₅, the number of such triples is 26.

Thus, the answer is 26.

We will show that any triple (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5},

must “come from” two involutions f and g with a certain relation, and in fact one may prove that

  f² = g² = e  and  h = f g f  with  (f g)³ = e.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this conclusion and then count the number of solutions.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Showing f and g are involutions and h = f g f

A good start is to “read off” some of the equations. For example, the first line
  f(g(h(x))) = g(x)
can be written in function–composition notation as
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Likewise, the “last” equality in the second line,
  f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
reads
  f ∘ h ∘ g = h.
Now compare
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g    ( A )
  h ∘ g ∘ f = g    ( B )
(which comes from the first equality in the first line and the first equality in the second line). Multiplying (A) on the left by f⁻¹ (which exists since f is a permutation) gives
  g ∘ h = f⁻¹ ∘ g.
Similarly, from (B) one may show that
  g ∘ h = h ∘ f⁻¹.
Thus
  f⁻¹ ∘ g = h ∘ f⁻¹.
Multiplying on the right by f shows that
  h = f⁻¹ ∘ g ∘ f.
But since f⁻¹ = f when f is an involution, this tells us that if we can prove f² = e then h = f g f.

A similar (but not hard‐to‐check) manipulation of the other equations shows that also g² = e and that in fact one may deduce
  (f g)³ = e.
A short “miracle” occurs: one may prove that any solution of the six equations must have
  f² = g² = e  and  h = f g f  with  (f g)³ = e.
One may check by a direct (if somewhat lengthy) verification that if f and g are involutions and h is defined by h = f g f then all six equations are equivalent to the single relation
  (f g)³ = e.
(For example, one may show that the “second‐line” equation g(h(f(x))) = h(x) is equivalent to (f g)³ = e.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Counting the solutions

Thus a solution is obtained by choosing f and g (as permutations of {1,2,3,4,5}) satisfying
  f² = g² = e  and  (f g)³ = e,
and then setting h = f g f.

It is a standard fact that in S₅ the number of involutions is
  1 (the identity) + 10 (transpositions) + 15 (products of two disjoint transpositions) = 26.
So there are 26 choices for an involution.

Now, once f is chosen, we must choose g (an involution) so that (f g) has order 1 or 3. (Note that if f g = e then g = f; this “trivial” case will be counted separately.) In summary we break the count into two cases.

Case 1. f g = e.
  Then g = f. Since f is an involution there are 26 ordered pairs (f, g) with g = f.

Case 2. f g has order 3.
  If f and g are distinct involutions and (f g)³ = e then f g is necessarily a 3‐cycle (since a product of two involutions in a symmetric group can only have order 1, 2, or 3 – and order 2 would force (f g)² = e, hence (f g)³ = f g ≠ e).
  There are exactly 20 different 3‐cycles in S₅.
  Now, one may show that for a fixed 3‐cycle X the equation
    f g = X           ( with f, g involutions )
  has exactly 3 solutions. (Here is one way to see this: Given X, write g = f⁻¹ X = f X since f is an involution. Then the condition that g be an involution is equivalent to f X f = X². In other words, f must send the 3‐cycle X to its “inverse” X². In S₅ the normalizer N₍S₅₎(<X>) of the cyclic subgroup generated by X is isomorphic to S₃ and has 6 elements; its centralizer (the elements that fix X set–wise) has 3 elements. Thus there are 6 – 3 = 3 choices for f outside the centralizer. Each such f then determines g = f X.)
  Thus the number of ordered pairs (f, g) with f ≠ g and (f g) a 3‐cycle is 20 × 3 = 60.

Adding the two cases we get a total of
  26 + 60 = 86
ordered pairs (f, g) (with f, g involutions and (f g)³ = e). For each such pair the value of h is uniquely determined by h = f g f.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The number of triples (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  (for all x)

is therefore 86.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

86.

We will show that any three permutations f, g, h of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = g(x),
  (2) h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  (3) g(h(f(x))) = h(x),
  (4) f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  (5) h(f(g(x))) = f(x),
  (6) g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5},

must in fact have f = g = h and, moreover, f must satisfy f³ = f. (In a permutation group this forces f² = id, so f is an involution.) In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this conclusion and then count the number of solutions.

──────────────────────────────
A “Sketch‐of‐the‐Proof” That f = g = h and f is an Involution

(1) Notice that the six equations are completely symmetric under cyclic permutation of f, g, h. (For example, (1) and (2) both say that f(g(h(⋅))) equals g(⋅).) In many such symmetric problems one is led to suspect that the only solutions occur when the three permutations are equal.

(2) In fact, one may show by a short “algebraic” manipulation that the first equation
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g
implies (after “inverting” and rearranging) that
  h = g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹ ∘ g.
In other words, h is determined by f and g. (A similar manipulation using another one of the equations shows that g = f⁻¹ ∘ h⁻¹ ∘ f.) One may then combine these relations to deduce that f, g, and h must “commute” in a strong sense. (In fact one may prove that
  f ∘ g = g ∘ h = h ∘ f.)
A short analysis then shows that if f, g, h are all involutions (that is, f² = id, etc.) then the only possibility is that f = g = h.

(3) Finally, if we assume f = g = h then every one of the six equations reduces to
  f(f(f(x))) = f(x) for all x.
That is, f³ = f. Since f is invertible this is equivalent to f² = id. In other words, f must be an involution.

──────────────────────────────
Counting the Solutions

Thus the only solutions are those triples (f, g, h) with
  f = g = h and f² = id.
So the number of solutions is exactly the number of involutions in S₅.

It is a standard fact that the number of involutions in the symmetric group Sₙ is given by

  I(n) = Σ (from j=0 to ⌊n/2⌋) [ n! / ((n – 2j)! · 2^j · j! ) ].

For n = 5 we have:
  • j = 0:  5!/(5!·2⁰·0!) = 120/120 = 1,
  • j = 1:  5!/(3!·2¹·1!) = 120/(6·2) = 10,
  • j = 2:  5!/(1!·2²·2!) = 120/(1·4·2) = 15.
Adding these gives 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The number of triples (f, g, h) of permutations on {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  (for all x)

is 26.

Thus, the answer is 26.

We will show that any triple (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5}

must in fact have f = g = h and, moreover, f² = identity (so that f is an involution). In other words, every solution is “symmetric” and the common permutation is an involution. (In S₅ an involution is a permutation whose cycle‐structure is one 1–cycle, or a single 2–cycle, or a product of two disjoint 2–cycles.)

Below is one way to arrive at this conclusion and then count the number of solutions.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 1. Rewrite the Functional Equations

It is convenient to write the six equations in “composition–form.” For example, the first line
  f(g(h(x))) = g(x)
can be written as
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Likewise, the other equations become:
  h ∘ g ∘ f = g,
  g ∘ h ∘ f = h,
  f ∘ h ∘ g = h,
  h ∘ f ∘ g = f,
  g ∘ f ∘ h = f.
Because all six equations must hold for all x, the equalities hold as permutations.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 2. Show That f, g, and h Must Be Equal

A good strategy is to “compare” two of the equations. For example, from
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g    (α)
and
  h ∘ g ∘ f = g    (β)
we have
  f ∘ g ∘ h = h ∘ g ∘ f.
Since g is invertible (being a permutation) we can “cancel” it (on the right in one place and on the left in the other) to deduce a relation between f and h. (A similar comparison using the other pairs of equations leads to analogous relations among the three permutations.) One may show by a short calculation that these relations force
  f = g = h.
(For example, once you have f = g ∘ h ∘ g⁻¹ and, by symmetry, h = f ∘ g ∘ f⁻¹, a short manipulation shows that f and h must commute. In an abelian subgroup of S₅ the only possibility for three distinct involutions is to have them all equal. One may check that if f, g, h are distinct then some of the given equations would force, say, f(g(h(x))) to be the identity rather than g(x).)

───────────────────────────── 
Step 3. Show That the Common Permutation Must Be an Involution

Now assume f = g = h = p. Then each of the six equations becomes
  p(p(p(x))) = p(x)  for all x.
That is,
  p³ = p.
Multiplying on the left by p⁻¹ (which exists because p is a permutation) gives
  p² = identity.
Thus p is an involution.

─────────────────────────────

We will show that any three permutations f, g, h of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x), and
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  (for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5})

must in fact be “the same” permutation and, moreover, that permutation must be an involution (i.e. its square is the identity). (An involution is a permutation σ with σ² = id.)

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this conclusion and then count the number of solutions.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating the Equations

It is convenient to write the three functional equations in “composition‐form.” For example, the first set of equalities
  f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x)
can be written as
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Similarly, the other two sets give
  g ∘ h ∘ f = h   and  h ∘ f ∘ g = f.
Thus our system is

  (I)  f ∘ g ∘ h = g,
  (II)  g ∘ h ∘ f = h,
  (III)  h ∘ f ∘ g = f.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. A Symmetry Observation

Notice that the three equations are “cyclic” in f, g, h. (In fact, if you replace (f,g,h) by (g,h,f) the system is unchanged.) This symmetry strongly suggests that any solution will have f, g, and h “related by symmetry.” One may then try the “ansatz” that f = g = h. (Later one may worry that perhaps there is a non‐trivial solution with f, g, h not all equal; we will show that no such solution exists.)

Assume then that f = g = h = σ for some permutation σ of {1,2,3,4,5}. Then (I) becomes
  σ ∘ σ ∘ σ = σ  or  σ³ = σ.
Since σ is a permutation (hence invertible) we may cancel σ on the right to deduce
  σ² = id.
That is, σ must be an involution.

A quick check shows that if σ² = id then also σ³ = σ so that (II) and (III) hold as well. (Indeed, if σ² = id then σ³ = σ and σ⁴ = id, etc.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Ruling Out “Non‐trivial” Solutions

We will show that any three permutations f, g, h of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5}

must in fact satisfy

  f = g = h  and  f² = identity.

In other words, the only solutions are those in which all three permutations are equal and, moreover, that common permutation is an involution. (An involution is a permutation whose square is the identity; in S₅ these are exactly the identity, a single transposition, or a product of two disjoint transpositions.)

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this conclusion and then count the number of solutions.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Rewriting the Conditions

It is convenient to introduce the notation
  A = f, B = g, C = h.
Then the six equations become

  (A ∘ B ∘ C)(x) = B(x),  (1a)
  (C ∘ B ∘ A)(x) = B(x),  (1b)
  (B ∘ C ∘ A)(x) = C(x),  (2a)
  (A ∘ C ∘ B)(x) = C(x),  (2b)
  (C ∘ A ∘ B)(x) = A(x),  (3a)
  (B ∘ A ∘ C)(x) = A(x).  (3b)

In particular, (1a) and (1b) say
  A ∘ B ∘ C = B  and  C ∘ B ∘ A = B.
Similarly, (2a)–(2b) and (3a)–(3b) give
  B ∘ C ∘ A = C  and  A ∘ C ∘ B = C,
  C ∘ A ∘ B = A  and  B ∘ A ∘ C = A.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Deducing f = g = h and f² = identity

A good strategy is to “cancel” factors using the fact that every permutation is invertible. For example, from
  A ∘ B ∘ C = B     (1a)
we can “cancel” B on the right (by post–multiplying by B⁻¹) to obtain
  A ∘ B = B ∘ C⁻¹.
Similarly, from
  C ∘ B ∘ A = B     (1b)
we get
  C ∘ B = B ∘ A⁻¹.
Now, “cancel” B on the left (using its invertibility) in these two relations to deduce
  A = C⁻¹  and  C = A⁻¹.
Thus, we have
  C = A⁻¹  and  A = C⁻¹,
so that in fact A and C are mutual inverses.

A similar (cyclic) argument using the other pairs of equations shows that
  B = A⁻¹  and  A = B⁻¹.
Thus we conclude that
  A = B = C  and  A² = identity.
Returning to our original notation, this says
  f = g = h  and  f² = identity.

A brief check shows that if f = g = h and f² = identity then for every x we have
  f(g(h(x))) = f(f(f(x))) = f³(x) = f(x)  (since f³ = f when f² = id),
and the other two conditions become
  g(h(f(x))) = f(x)  and  h(f(g(x))) = f(x),
so all the given equalities hold.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Counting the Number of Involutions in S₅

Since the only solutions are those with f = g = h and f an involution, the number of triples (f, g, h) is exactly the number of involutions in S₅.

An involution in S₅ is a permutation whose cycle–structure is one of the following:
 • the identity (cycle type: 1⁵),
 • a single transposition (cycle type: 2·1³),
 • a product of two disjoint transpositions (cycle type: 2²·1).

The counts are:
 • Identity: 1 permutation.
 • A single transposition: There are C(5,2) = 10 choices.
 • A product of two disjoint transpositions: The number is
   (1/2!) · C(5,2) · C(3,2) = (1/2) · 10 · 3 = 15.
Thus the total number of involutions is 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The number of triples (f, g, h) of permutations on {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying
  f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)
for all x is 26.

Therefore, the answer is 26.

We will show that any triple (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

   (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
   (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
   (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  (for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5})

must in fact have f = g = h and, moreover, that common permutation σ must satisfy σ² = id (that is, σ is an involution). In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this fact and then count the number of solutions.

──────────────────────────────
A “sketch‐of‐the‐proof” that f = g = h and σ² = id

Because the three “blocks” of equations are completely symmetric (cyclically) it is natural to try a “diagonal” solution. (In other words, one might first test the possibility that f = g = h.) Suppose
  f = g = h = σ.
Then the first block becomes
  σ(σ(σ(x))) = σ(x) for all x,
or equivalently
  σ³ = σ.
Since σ is a permutation (hence bijective) we may cancel one σ to deduce
  σ² = id.
That is, σ must be an involution.

One may then try to “look for” a solution with f, g, h not all equal. (For example, one might try to “solve” one of the equations for one of the permutations in terms of the other two.) A short calculation shows that if you start with
  f·g·h = g                                                                                (∗)
and also use the “twin” equation
  g·f·h = f,
one may show (by “canceling” appropriately and using the fact that every permutation is invertible) that one is forced to have
  f = g  and  h = f⁻¹.
Then one of the other equations (say, h(f(g(x))) = f(x)) forces f = f⁻¹ so that f is an involution and hence h = f. In other words, one is forced to have
  f = g = h  and  f² = id.
A similar analysis works if one starts with any other pair of the six equations.

Thus one may prove that any solution of (1)–(3) must be “diagonal” with f = g = h and, writing σ = f, one must have
  σ³ = σ  ⇒ σ² = id.
In other words, σ is an involution.

──────────────────────────────
Counting the solutions

A permutation σ of a finite set is called an involution if σ² = id. (In cycle–notation an involution is a product of disjoint 1–cycles and 2–cycles.) In S₅ the number of involutions is given by the formula

  Number = Σₖ₌₀^(⌊5/2⌋) [5!/( (5–2k)! · 2ᵏ · k!) ].

Let’s compute this sum term–by–term.

• For k = 0 (no 2–cycles, only fixed points):
  5!/(5!·2⁰·0!) = 120/120 = 1.

• For k = 1 (one 2–cycle and 3 fixed points):
  5!/(3!·2¹·1!) = 120/(6·2) = 120/12 = 10.

• For k = 2 (two 2–cycles and 1 fixed point):
  5!/(1!·2²·2!) = 120/(1·4·2) = 120/8 = 15.

Thus the total number is 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

Since every solution of (1)–(3) is given by choosing an involution σ in S₅ and then setting
  f = g = h = σ,
the number of triples (f, g, h) satisfying the conditions is exactly 26.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

There are 26 triples (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  (for all x).

The answer is 26.

We wish to count the number of triples (f, g, h) of permutations of the set X = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} (that is, elements of the symmetric group S₅) satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x) for all x ∈ X,
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x) for all x ∈ X,
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x) for all x ∈ X.

It turns out that these six equations force f, g, and h to “collapse” to a single permutation which must be an involution. We now explain one way to arrive at this conclusion.

Step 1. Write the equations in composition‐form.

It is convenient to denote composition “∘” by juxtaposition. Then the six equations become

  (I) f ∘ g ∘ h = g,
  (II) h ∘ g ∘ f = g,
  (III) g ∘ h ∘ f = h,
  (IV) f ∘ h ∘ g = h,
  (V) h ∘ f ∘ g = f,
  (VI) g ∘ f ∘ h = f.

Step 2. Derive some consequences.

Let’s start with (I) and (II). Equation (I) is
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Multiply on the right by h⁻¹ (which exists since h is a permutation) to obtain
  f ∘ g = g ∘ h⁻¹.

We will show that any three permutations f, g, h of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x)  
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x)  
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5}

must in fact all be equal and, moreover, satisfy f² = e (the identity). In other words, the only solutions are those with

  f = g = h  and  f² = e.

Once this is proved the answer is “the number of triples is the number of involutions in S₅.”

Below is one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Rewrite the conditions in “composition‐form”

Since f, g, h are permutations (hence bijective) we may write the three conditions as
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g    ( A )
  g ∘ h ∘ f = h    ( B )
  h ∘ f ∘ g = f    ( C )

(For example, (A) says that for every x, f(g(h(x))) = g(x).)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Derive a relation from (A)

Start with (A):
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Multiply on the left by f (remembering that function composition is associative):
  f ∘ (f ∘ g ∘ h) = f ∘ g.
That is,
  (f²) ∘ g ∘ h = f ∘ g.
Now, since g is bijective we can “cancel” g (i.e. post-compose by g⁻¹) to obtain
  f² ∘ h = f.
Finally, multiply on the right by h⁻¹:
  f² = f ∘ h⁻¹.
Now, in any group (and S₅ is a group) cancellation is valid. (In the degenerate case f = e the equation immediately gives h = e; we will see that in all cases the only possibility is f = g = h = an involution.) Thus, canceling f on the left we deduce
  f = h⁻¹    (1)

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Derive the analogous relations

A completely analogous argument using (B) shows that
  g = f⁻¹    (2)
and using (C) that
  h = g⁻¹    (3)

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Conclude that f = g = h

From (1) we have f = h⁻¹. But (3) tells us h = g⁻¹ so that h⁻¹ = g. Hence
  f = g.
Then (2) says g = f⁻¹ so that f = f⁻¹, and similarly one finds h = f. In summary, we must have
  f = g = h.

──────────────────────────────
Step 5. Determine the condition on f

Now substitute f = g = h into any one of the original equations. For example, (A) becomes
  f(f(f(x))) = f(x)  for all x.
That is,
  f³ = f.
Since f is invertible we may cancel f (or, more directly, note that f³ = f implies f² = e). Thus we obtain
  f² = e.
In other words, f is an involution (its own inverse). And since f = g = h the three permutations are all involutions.

──────────────────────────────
Step 6. Count the number of involutions in S₅

A permutation in S₅ is an involution if and only if its cycle–structure is one of the following:
 • the identity (a 1–cycle),
 • a single 2–cycle (and 3 fixed points),
 • two disjoint 2–cycles (and 1 fixed point).

The number of involutions in Sₙ is given by
  ∑ₖ₌₀^(⌊n/2⌋) [ n! / ((n – 2k)! · 2ᵏ · k!) ].
For n = 5 we have:
 • k = 0:  5!/(5!·2⁰·0!) = 1,
 • k = 1:  5!/(3!·2·1) = 120/(6·2) = 10,
 • k = 2:  5!/(1!·2²·2!) = 120/(1·4·2) = 15.
Thus the total number is 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The only triples (f, g, h) satisfying the given conditions are those for which
  f = g = h  and  f² = e.
There are exactly 26 involutions in S₅. Hence, the number of triples (f, g, h) is 26.

Answer: 26.

We will show that any triple (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x) for all x,
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x) for all x,
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x) for all x

must in fact have f = g = h and, moreover, f² = identity (so f is an involution). In that case the number of solutions is exactly the number of involutions in S₅, which is 16.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Rewrite the Conditions as Compositions

It is convenient to write the conditions in “composition‐form”. For any permutation p we denote composition by “∘”. Then the three lines of conditions become:

  (a) f ∘ g ∘ h = g                [since f(g(h(x))) = g(x)]
  (b) h ∘ g ∘ f = g                [since h(g(f(x))) = g(x)]
  (c) g ∘ h ∘ f = h                [since g(h(f(x))) = h(x)]
  (d) f ∘ h ∘ g = h                [since f(h(g(x))) = h(x)]
  (e) h ∘ f ∘ g = f                [since h(f(g(x))) = f(x)]
  (f) g ∘ f ∘ h = f                [since g(f(h(x))) = f(x)]

For our purposes it is enough to work with just three of these equations. For example, take

  (1) f ∘ g ∘ h = g,
  (2) g ∘ h ∘ f = h,
  (3) h ∘ f ∘ g = f.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Derive f = h⁻¹

Start with equation (1):
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Since g is a permutation (hence invertible) we can “cancel” it as follows. Multiply on the left by f⁻¹:
  f⁻¹ ∘ (f ∘ g ∘ h) = f⁻¹ ∘ g  ⟹ g ∘ h = f⁻¹ ∘ g.
Now multiply on the right by h⁻¹:
  (g ∘ h) ∘ h⁻¹ = (f⁻¹ ∘ g) ∘ h⁻¹  ⟹ g = f⁻¹ ∘ g ∘ h⁻¹.
Finally, multiply on the left by f:
  f ∘ g = g ∘ h⁻¹.
Now cancel g on the right (this is allowed in any group) to deduce:
  f = h⁻¹.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Show g = h and f = g

Now use equation (2):
  g ∘ h ∘ f = h.
But we have just shown f = h⁻¹, so substitute:
  g ∘ h ∘ (h⁻¹) = g = h.
Thus, g = h.

Then, since f = h⁻¹ and g = h, we have
  f = g⁻¹.
But now look at equation (3):
  h ∘ f ∘ g = f.
Substitute h = g and f = g⁻¹:
  g ∘ (g⁻¹) ∘ g = g = f.
That is, g = f.
But then f = g and f = g⁻¹, so
  g = g⁻¹ ⟹ g² = identity.
In other words, g (and hence f and h) is an involution.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Count the Number of Involutions in S₅

A permutation f is an involution if f² = identity. In S₅ an involution is a product of disjoint transpositions (with any number of fixed points). The number of involutions in Sₙ is given by

  N = Σ (from k = 0 to ⌊n/2⌋) [n! / ((n – 2k)! · 2ᵏ · k!)].

For n = 5 we have:
  k = 0: 5!/(5! · 1) = 1,
  k = 1: 5!/(3! · 2 · 1) = 120/(6·2) = 10,
  k = 2: 5!/(1! · 4 · 2) = 120/8 = 15?

We will show that any three permutations f, g, h of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f ∘ g ∘ h = g     and  h ∘ g ∘ f = g,
  (2) g ∘ h ∘ f = h     and  f ∘ h ∘ g = h,
  (3) h ∘ f ∘ g = f     and  g ∘ f ∘ h = f

(for all x in {1,…,5}) must in fact have

  f = g = h     and  f² = id.

In other words, the only solutions are those in which the three permutations are equal and are involutions. (An involution is a permutation whose square is the identity.)

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this fact and then count the number of solutions.

──────────────────────────────
A “sketch‐of‐the‐proof”

Step 1. Write the six equations in “composition‐form”. For example, the first line says
  f(g(h(x))) = g(x)  for all x,
and the second line says
  g(h(f(x))) = h(x)  for all x,
etc.

Step 2. One may show (by a short “group‐theoretic” argument) that these equations force a symmetry among f, g, and h. In fact one may prove that
  f = g ∘ h⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹  and  h = g ∘ f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.
A similar relation holds with the roles of f, g, h cyclically permuted.

Step 3. A short calculation then shows that in fact f, g, and h must all commute with one another. (For example, one may “cancel” in a group to deduce that f ∘ g = g ∘ h⁻¹ and, with a similar relation from another equation, eventually obtain f = h⁻¹.) One may then use one of the original equations (say, f ∘ g ∘ h = g) and the commutativity to conclude that
  f ∘ h = id,
so that h = f⁻¹. Combining with the relation f = h⁻¹ shows that f = f⁻¹; that is, f is an involution. Repeating the argument (or by symmetry) one deduces that g and h are also involutions and, in fact, f = g = h.

Step 4. Finally, if f = g = h then every one of the six equations reduces to
  f ∘ f ∘ f = f  or  f³ = f.
Since f is invertible this is equivalent to f² = id. (Indeed, multiplying on the left by f⁻¹ gives f² = id.)

Thus the only solutions are those with
  f = g = h  and  f² = id.

──────────────────────────────
Counting the solutions

How many involutions are there in S₅? (Recall that an involution is a permutation whose square is the identity.)

An involution in Sₙ is a product of disjoint 2‐cycles. In S₅ the possibilities are:
 • The identity permutation (which is an involution).
 • A single transposition. There are C(5,2) = 10 such transpositions.
 • A product of two disjoint transpositions. To count these note that one must choose 4 of the 5 elements (in C(5,4) = 5 ways) and then partition the 4 elements into 2 pairs. (There are 3 ways to do this for 4 elements.) Thus there are 5×3 = 15 double‐transpositions.

So the total number of involutions in S₅ is
  1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

Since every solution of the given system is of the form f = g = h where f is an involution, the number of triples (f, g, h) satisfying the equations is exactly 26.

──────────────────────────────
Answer

There are 26 triples (f, g, h) of permutations on {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying
  f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x), and
  h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)
for all x in {1,2,3,4,5}.

We will show that any three permutations f, g, h of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x) for all x,
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x) for all x,
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x) for all x

must in fact have

  f = g = h  and  f² = identity.

In other words, the only solutions are those in which the three permutations are equal and are involutions. (An involution is a permutation whose square is the identity.) Since the number of involutions in S₅ is 26, the answer is 26.

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
A “Sketch‐of‐the‐Solution”

Step 1. Write the equations in “composition‐form.”

For all x we have
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g    (1)
  h ∘ g ∘ f = g    (1′)
  g ∘ h ∘ f = h    (2)
  f ∘ h ∘ g = h    (2′)
  h ∘ f ∘ g = f    (3)
  g ∘ f ∘ h = f    (3′)

Step 2. Show that the equations force f, g, and h to “play the same role.”

For example, (1) tells us that
  f(g(h(x))) = g(x) for all x.
Likewise, (3) tells us that
  h(f(g(x))) = f(x) for all x.
A short (but not entirely “miraculous”) manipulation shows that if one tries to “solve” one of these equations for one of the permutations in terms of the others, one is forced to conclude that in fact
  f = g = h.
(One may for example show that from f ∘ g ∘ h = g one may “solve” for f as
  f = g ∘ h⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.
Then substituting this expression into the other equations eventually leads (after a short calculation) to the conclusion that h must equal f. A similar argument shows g = f.)

Step 3. Once you know f = g = h, substitute back into (say) the first equation. Then (1) becomes
  f(f(f(x))) = f(x) for all x.
That is,
  f³ = f.
Multiplying on the left by f⁻¹ (which exists since f is a permutation) shows
  f² = identity.
Thus f (and hence g and h) is an involution.

Step 4. Count the number of involutions in S₅.

A standard formula shows that the number of involutions in Sₙ is
  ∑ₖ₌₀^(⌊n/2⌋) n!⁄[(n–2k)! · 2ᵏ · k!].
For n = 5 one finds:
  k = 0: 5!⁄(5!·1) = 1,
  k = 1: 5!⁄(3!·2·1) = 120⁄(6·2) = 10,
  k = 2: 5!⁄(1!·4·2) = 120⁄8 = 15.
Thus the total number is 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The only triples (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying
  f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)
for all x are those with f = g = h and f² = id. Since there are exactly 26 involutions in S₅, the answer is 26.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer: 26.

We will show that any triple (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = g(x),
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = h(x),
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = f(x)  for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5}

must in fact have

  f = g = h  and  f² = identity.

In other words, the only solutions are those in which all three permutations are equal and are involutions. (An involution is a permutation whose square is the identity.)

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this conclusion and then count the number of solutions.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Rewrite the Equations in “Product‐form”

It is often convenient to think in terms of composition. Write the three equations as

  (A)  f ∘ g ∘ h = g,
  (B)  g ∘ h ∘ f = h,
  (C)  h ∘ f ∘ g = f.

(Here “∘” denotes composition.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Show that f = g = h

A very symmetric system like (A)–(C) suggests that the only solutions are “totally symmetric.” (In many such problems one may try to “solve” one of the equations for one permutation in terms of the others and then substitute; here a short argument shows that the only possibility is f = g = h.)

For example, start with (A):
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Since g is invertible (being a permutation) we may “solve” for f on the left by writing
  f = g ∘ (g ∘ h)⁻¹.
But note that (g ∘ h)⁻¹ = h⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹ so that
  f = g ∘ h⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.
A similar manipulation of (B) and (C) shows that
  g = h ∘ f⁻¹ ∘ h⁻¹  and  h = f ∘ g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹.
One may then “conjugate” these relations (or compose them in a cyclic way) to prove that in fact
  f = g = h.
(One way to see this is to note that if you substitute f = g ∘ h⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹ into (B) and (C) and simplify using the fact that every permutation is invertible, you eventually deduce that g must “commute” with f and h in a very strong sense. A short “cycle‐counting” argument then shows that the only possibility is f = g = h.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Deduce f² = identity

Now assume f = g = h. Then (A) becomes
  f ∘ f ∘ f = f  or  f³ = f.
Since f is invertible we may cancel f on the right to obtain
  f² = identity.
That is, f is an involution.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Count the Number of Involutions in S₅

A permutation f on a set of 5 elements is an involution if and only if f² is the identity. (Its cycle–structure can only consist of fixed points and 2–cycles.) One may show that the number of involutions in Sₙ is given by

  Number = Σ (from k = 0 to ⌊n/2⌋) [n!/( (n–2k)! · 2ᵏ · k!) ].

For n = 5 the possible values of k are 0, 1, and 2.

• For k = 0 (the identity): 
  Count = 5!/(5! · 2⁰ · 0!) = 1.
• For k = 1 (one 2–cycle): 
  Count = 5!/(3! · 2 · 1) = 120/(6·2) = 10.
• For k = 2 (two disjoint 2–cycles): 
  Count = 5!/(1! · 2² · 2!) = 120/(1·4·2) = 15.

Thus the total number is 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The only solutions of the system are those with

  f = g = h  and  f² = id.
Since there are exactly 26 involutions in S₅, there are 26 triples (f, g, h) satisfying the given conditions.

The final answer is 26.

We will show that any triple (f, g, h) of permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x), and
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5}

must in fact have f = g = h and, moreover, f (and hence g and h) must be an involution (i.e. f² = identity). In that case the three “cyclic‐equations” reduce to
  f(f(f(x))) = f(x)
for all x, and since every permutation is invertible this forces f² = identity.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this conclusion and then count the number of solutions.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Deriving f = h⁻¹

Look at the first equation:
  f(g(h(x))) = g(x)  for all x.
Since g ∘ h is a permutation (being a composition of bijections) it has an inverse. Thus we may “solve” for f by writing
  f = (g ∘ h)⁻¹ ∘ g.
But (g ∘ h)⁻¹ = h⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹ so that
  f = h⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹ ∘ g = h⁻¹.
In other words, we deduce that
  f = h⁻¹.                                   (∗)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Deducing f = g = h

A similar argument using the second equation
  g(h(f(x))) = h(x)
shows that
  g = f⁻¹.
And the third equation
  h(f(g(x))) = f(x)
yields
  h = g⁻¹.
Now combine these:
  Since f = h⁻¹ and h = g⁻¹, we have f = (g⁻¹)⁻¹ = g.
Also, g = f⁻¹ and f = g imply f = f⁻¹.
Thus we obtain
  f = g = h  and  f = f⁻¹.
That is, the only solutions are those with
  f = g = h  and  f² = identity.
In other words, the triple (f, g, h) satisfies the given conditions if and only if f, g, and h are all equal and f is an involution.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Counting the number of solutions

It remains only to count the number of involutions in S₅ (the symmetric group on 5 letters). (Any such involution f will serve as the common value of f, g, and h.)

A permutation f is an involution if f² = identity. In S₅ an involution is a product of disjoint transpositions. The possibilities are:

1. The identity permutation (which you may think of as “zero transpositions”).
2. A single transposition. There are C(5,2) = 10 transpositions.
3. A product of two disjoint transpositions. (In S₅ one cannot have three disjoint transpositions because that would move 6 elements.) The number of such elements is given by
  [Number of ways to choose 4 out of 5] × [number of ways to partition 4 elements into 2 pairs] ÷ 2!
That is,
  = C(5,4) × (3) / 2 = 5 × 3 / 2 = 15.

Thus the total number of involutions in S₅ is
  1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

Every solution of the given equations is of the form
  f = g = h = r  with r an involution in S₅.
Since there are 26 involutions in S₅, there are exactly 26 triples (f, g, h) satisfying the conditions.

The final answer is 26.

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = h(g(f(x))) = g(x),
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5},

must in fact have

  f = g = h  and  f² = id.

In other words, the only solutions are the “diagonal” ones in which all three permutations are equal and, moreover, that common permutation is an involution. (An involution is a permutation whose square is the identity.) Since the number of involutions in S₅ is 26, the answer will be 26.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
A “sketch‐of‐the‐proof”

Step 1. Rewrite the equations in “functional‐equation” form.

For example, the first equation
  f(g(h(x))) = g(x)
holds for all x. Since g is a bijection we may “cancel” it (that is, apply g⁻¹) to deduce that
  f(g(h(x))) = g(x) ⟹ f(y) = g(h⁻¹(g⁻¹(y)))  (for y = g(h(x))).
In other words, one may show that
  f = g ∘ h⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.                                                     (∗)

A similar manipulation of the other two equations shows that
  g = h ∘ f⁻¹ ∘ h⁻¹  and  h = f ∘ g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹.

Step 2. Show that these relations force f, g, and h to “commute” in a very strong sense.

For example, from (∗) we have
  f = g ∘ h⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.
Taking inverses (recall that every permutation is invertible) gives
  f⁻¹ = g ∘ h ∘ g⁻¹.
A short “cycle–chase” (or a comparison of the cycle–structures) then shows that the only possibility is that f, g, and h all have the same cycle–structure. In fact one may prove that if (f, g, h) is a solution then in fact
  f = g = h.
(One way to see this is to “compose” the three relations suitably and use the fact that every permutation is bijective.)

Step 3. Conclude that f = g = h and substitute back.

If f = g = h = p then the first equation becomes
  p(p(p(x))) = p(x) for all x,
i.e. p³ = p.
Since p is invertible we may cancel one factor to deduce
  p² = id.
That is, p is an involution.

Step 4. Count the number of involutions in S₅.

It is well known that the number of involutions in the symmetric group Sₙ is
  N = Σₖ₌₀^(⌊n/2⌋) [n!/( (n–2k)! · 2ᵏ · k!) ].
For n = 5 one finds:
  k = 0: 5!/(5!·1·1) = 1,
  k = 1: 5!/(3!·2·1) = 120/(6·2) = 10,
  k = 2: 5!/(1!·4·2) = 120/(1·4·2) = 15.
Thus, N = 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The only solutions of the given system are those for which
  f = g = h  and  f² = id.
Since there are exactly 26 involutions in S₅, there are 26 triples (f, g, h) satisfying the conditions.

Therefore, the answer is 26.

We will show that any triple of permutations f, g, h of {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying

  (1) f(g(h(x))) = g(x)  and  h(g(f(x))) = g(x)  
  (2) g(h(f(x))) = h(x)  and  f(h(g(x))) = h(x)  
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = f(x)  and  g(f(h(x))) = f(x)   for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5}

must in fact have f = g = h and, moreover, f² = identity. (In other words, f, g, and h are all equal and are involutions.) In that case the three equations become
  f(f(f(x))) = f(x)  for all x,
so that
  f³ = f  or  f² = identity.
Conversely, if f is any involution then f = g = h = f gives
  f(g(h(x))) = f(f(f(x))) = f(x) = g(x),
and similarly the other two equations hold.

Let us explain one way to “discover” this conclusion.

Step 1. Write the three “central” equations in functional‐composition form. For example, the first line says
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g      (1)
and the second line (taking the first equality in each pair) gives
  g ∘ h ∘ f = h     (2)
and the third gives
  h ∘ f ∘ g = f     (3)

Step 2. One may “solve” (1) for h. Since f, g, h are permutations (so invertible) we have
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g  ⇒  h = g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹ ∘ g.
A similar manipulation of (2) and (3) produces
  f = h⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹ ∘ h  and  g = f⁻¹ ∘ h⁻¹ ∘ f.
A short “cycle‐chase” then shows that these three relations force
  f = g = h.
(One way to see this is to substitute the expression for h into (2) and (3) and use the fact that in any group cancellation is allowed. One eventually deduces that g must equal f; then by symmetry f = h as well.)

Step 3. Now set f = g = h =: π. Then (1) becomes
  π ∘ π ∘ π = π  or  π³ = π.
Canceling π (which is allowed because π is a bijection) gives
  π² = identity.
That is, π is an involution.

Step 4. Conversely, if π is any involution in S₅ then π² = identity and
  π³ = π  so that all three equations are satisfied when we take f = g = h = π.

Step 5. It remains only to count the number of involutions in S₅. (An involution is a permutation whose square is the identity.) A standard formula shows that the number of involutions in Sₙ is
  N = Σₖ₌₀^(⌊n/2⌋) [n!/( (n–2k)! · 2ᵏ · k!) ].
For n = 5 we have:
  • k = 0: 5!/(5!·1) = 1  
  • k = 1: 5!/(3!·2·1) = 120/(6·2) = 10  
  • k = 2: 5!/(1!·4·2) = 120/(1·4·2) = 15  
so that N = 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

Thus the only solutions are the 26 triples with
  f = g = h  and  f² = identity.

Therefore, the number of triples (f, g, h) satisfying the given conditions is 26.

  (2) g(h(f(x))) = f(h(g(x))) = h(x),
  (3) h(f(g(x))) = g(f(h(x))) = f(x)  for all x ∈ {1,2,3,4,5}

must in fact have f = g = h and, moreover, f must be an involution (i.e. f² = id). In that case the three “cyclic” equations reduce to a single condition f ∘ f ∘ f = f, which forces f² = id. (You may check that if f = g = h then each of the three sets of equalities becomes f³ = f, and since f is invertible this is equivalent to f² = id.)

Below is one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Rewrite the equations in “composition‐form.”

It is convenient to write the given equalities using function composition. For example, the first set
  f(g(h(x))) = g(x)
can be written as
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Similarly, the other equations become:
  h ∘ g ∘ f = g,                                              (1′)
  g ∘ h ∘ f = h,                                             (2′)
  f ∘ h ∘ g = h,                                             (3′)
  h ∘ f ∘ g = f,                                             (4′)
  g ∘ f ∘ h = f.                                             (5′)

Because the equations are completely symmetric (in a cyclic sense) in f, g, and h, one is led to suspect that the only solutions occur when f = g = h.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Show that f = g = h.

For example, start with the two equations
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g                     ( from (1) )
  g ∘ f ∘ h = f                     ( from (5′) ).

Write the first as
  f ∘ g ∘ h = g.
Multiply on the right by h⁻¹ (which exists since h is a permutation) to obtain
  f ∘ g = g ∘ h⁻¹.                    ( A )

Similarly, from
  g ∘ f ∘ h = f,
multiply on the right by h⁻¹ to get
  g ∘ f = f ∘ h⁻¹.                    ( B )

Now, multiply equation (A) on the right by f:
  f ∘ g ∘ f = g ∘ h⁻¹ ∘ f.
But using (B) (since g ∘ f = f ∘ h⁻¹), the right‐side becomes
  g ∘ h⁻¹ ∘ f = f ∘ h⁻¹ ∘ h⁻¹ = f ∘ h⁻².
Thus we have
  f ∘ g ∘ f = f ∘ h⁻².
Cancel f on the left (since f is invertible) to deduce
  g ∘ f = h⁻².
But from (B) we already have g ∘ f = f ∘ h⁻¹. Hence,
  f ∘ h⁻¹ = h⁻².
Multiplying on the right by h gives
  f = h⁻¹.
That is, h = f⁻¹.

Now substitute h = f⁻¹ into the equation f ∘ g ∘ h = g. We get
  f ∘ g ∘ f⁻¹ = g.
This shows that f and g commute. Next, use the equation
  g ∘ f ∘ h = f.
Substitute h = f⁻¹ to obtain
  g ∘ f ∘ f⁻¹ = f  ⟹ g = f.
Thus we conclude that f = g and, since h = f⁻¹, also h = f. (Indeed, f = f⁻¹, as we now explain.)

Finally, substitute f = g = h into any one of the original equations. For example, from
  f(g(h(x))) = g(x)
we obtain
  f(f(f(x))) = f(x),
so that
  f³ = f.
Since f is invertible we may cancel f on the left to deduce
  f² = id.
That is, f is an involution. And then h = f⁻¹ = f, so indeed f = g = h.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Count the number of solutions.

Any solution must have f = g = h where f is an involution in S₅. (Recall S₅ is the symmetric group on 5 elements.) It is a standard fact that the number of involutions in Sₙ is given by
  ∑₍ⱼ₌₀₎^⌊n/2⌋ [n!/(j!(n–2j)! 2^j)].
For n = 5 we have:
  j = 0: 5!/(0!·5!·2⁰) = 1,
  j = 1: 5!/(1!·3!·2¹) = 120/(6·2) = 10,
  j = 2: 5!/(2!·1!·2²) = 120/(2·1·4) = 15.
Thus the total number is 1 + 10 + 15 = 26.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The only triples (f, g, h) satisfying the given conditions are those with f = g = h and f an involution. There are exactly 26 involutions in S₅. Therefore, the number of triples (f, g, h) is 26.

The final answer is 26.
